bib.title: AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench", Toledo, Hambardzumyan, Josifoski, et al. (FAIR at Meta, UCL), arXiv 2507.02554 preprint, dated July 3, 2025.

COVERAGE: Extracted all 34 pages with pypdf (100,215 chars) to /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/aira2/full.txt. I read in full: Appendix A, B, C, D, E (E.1 to E.6), F, G, H, I, J, K and L, plus the Table 3 per-task rows. I also re-read the main-text passages that bear on your three claims: abstract, Sec 3.3 and 3.4, Sec 5.1 to 5.3, and the conclusion and limitations. Figures 14 to 17 are graphics, and their numbers are not extractable. The text has no Appendix E.7 or later; E ends at Crossover. There is no separate Appendix of "operator prompts" beyond E.2 to E.6.

CLAIMS (ranked)

(a) The validation vs test gap is in PERCENTAGE POINTS (absolute medal rate), even though the text prints "%".
- claim: Using the test score for search and selection (Test/Test) instead of validation (Val/Val) raises the medal rate by 9.4 / 12.4 / 15 / 16.6 for AIRA-MCTS / AIRA-Evo / AIRA-Greedy / AIDE-Greedy. These are absolute points.
  number: 9.4, 12.4, 15, 16.6
  setup: MLE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-R1 agents, 24h, 20 seeds. Fig 6a is stated as R1 only.
  quote: "searching based on the test score instead of the validation score improves performance by 9.4 % and 12.4 % forAIRAmcts and AIRAevo. The gap is even higher for the agents using a greedy search policy, reaching 15 % forAIRAgreedy and 16.6 % forAIDEgreedy."
  where: p.10, Sec 5.3
- Evidence for points, not relative: the Fig 6a caption says "Bars depict the absolute performance gap". The conclusion says "would increase the medal rate by 9 to 13 % (absolute scale), depending on the search strategy" (p.12). I checked it against the bar labels, which are in the order Val/Val, Val/Test, Test/Test per agent. The extraction interleaves the labels: "39.8 51.4 43.0 56.1 45.5 54.5 47.0 56.6 56.4 55.0 60.5 56.4".
  My reconstruction, with x-axis order AIDE, Evo, Greedy, MCTS:
  - Val/Val: 39.8, 43.0, 45.5, 47.0.
  - Val/Test: 51.4, 56.1, 54.5, 56.6.
  - Test/Test: 56.4, 55.0, 60.5, 56.4.
  Checks: MCTS 56.4-47.0 = 9.4 (matches). Greedy 60.5-45.5 = 15.0 (matches). AIDE 56.4-39.8 = 16.6 (matches). Evo 55.0-43.0 = 12.0, not the 12.4 in the text. The 0.4 discrepancy is probably my label assignment or a typo; treat it as unresolved. Check the figure image if you cite 12.4 precisely.
- Note: the 9-to-13 range in the conclusion is the Test/Test minus Val/Val range. A different "9 to 13 absolute points" in Sec 5.3 is the Val/Test boost (final-node selection only).
  quote: "all agents achieve a performance boost of 9 to 13 absolute points."
  where: p.10

(a2) Most of the gap is final-node selection, not search guidance.
- quote: "comparingV al/Testwith Test/Test shows that oracle final-node selection eliminates the gap between the standard (V al/V al) and oracle (Test/Test) settings for bothAIRAmcts and AIRAevo. Even for the agents implementing the simpler greedy policy, selecting the best node in the final search graph closes more than 60 % of the gap."
  where: p.10
- Top-k remedy (Fig 6b, k=2..8):
  quote: "with as little as 3 top-k submissions agents achieve an additional 10 % of performance"
  where: p.11 (unit not stated; likely points)
- Greedy-AIRA reconstruction: 54.5 - 45.5 = 9.0 of 15.0, which is 60%. This matches ">60%" only roughly. For AIDE, 51.4 - 39.8 = 11.6 of 16.6, which is 70%.

(a3) The gap grows with time, and the AIRA operators shrink it.
- quote: "the agent's perceived performance (validation score) continues to improve over time, the true test performance plateaus, even slightly decreases over time."
  where: p.8, Fig 4a (AIDE-greedy)
- App J: "Compared to Fig. 4a, the agents using AIRA operators display a smaller gap between test and validation scores." (p.29)
- App C, 90-hour run (10 seeds per task): the quote below is from p.18. The text says 90 hours, while Fig 9's caption and the Limitations say 120 hours and 5 days. The paper is internally inconsistent here.
  quote: "AIRAgreedy continues to improve, ultimately achieving a peak medal rate of approximately 53%. This peak represents an absolute improvement of 6% over the highest performance attained with 24 hours of compute, translating into a relative gain of 12%. However, the agent's performance subsequently declines as overfitting begins to manifest."
  Also: "AIRAmcts begins to overfit and its performance subsequently deteriorates" at about 50 hours. Over the long horizon, "AIRAgreedy and AIRAmcts achieve a similar test-validation gap as AIDEgreedy."

(b) MCTS and evo give no gain with AIDE's operators. This holds, but only for AIDE's operators.
- Fig 3 values (R1): AIDE-greedy 39.77, no-memory 38.18, [OAI] o1-preview 35.23, MCTS c=0.0/0.25/0.50/0.75 = 36.36/35.45/35.00/34.55, AIDE-Evo 39.61. I assigned these by x-order, so the mapping is my reading of the figure labels.
  quote: "When limited to AIDE's operator setOAIDE, agents using more advances search policies (e.g., MCTS, evolutionary algorithms) gain no advantage, underscoring the operator set as the bottleneck."
  where: Fig 3 caption, p.7
  quote: "The resulting medal rates (Fig. 3) showed only marginal differences across allcUCT values... We observe the same limitation when performing the same operator replacement inAIRAevo."
  where: p.8
  Memory ablation: "both variants achieve nearly identical mean medal rates."
- With AIRA operators the policies do differ somewhat (Fig 5, R1 any-medal): Greedy 45.45, MCTS 47.05, Evo 42.73, AIDE 39.77.
  quote: "AIRAgreedy outperforms AIDEgreedy (45.5 % vs. 39.8 %), representing a 14 % relative improvement"
  quote: "AIRAmcts achieves the best performance, achieving state-of-the-art performance on MLE-bench Lite with an average medal rate of 47%."
  where: p.9
- Caveat: the per-policy differences are small, and 95% CIs (stratified bootstrap) are in Fig 5. Anytime rankings change over time: "Meaningful divergence in performance appears only after 19 hours" (p.10). App C says 15 hours, and the main text says 19, so these are inconsistent.
- App I on variance: "We recommend using a minimum of 10 seeds per task for moderate ranking stability, with 20 seeds preferred". Fig 11 shows the same method set re-ranked at 3, 5, 10 and 15 seeds. Gaps of 2 to 5 points between policies are within this noise.

(c) Setup. 22 tasks, 20 seeds, R1 and 24h are all confirmed.
- quote: "MLE-bench lite—a curated subset of 22 tasks selected from the full benchmark." (p.5, Sec 3.3)
- quote: "the agent is allowed a 24-hour wall-clock window. Within this period, each agent has a maximum runtime of 4 hours per code execution." (p.5)
- quote: "We conducted all the experiments with the full-sizedDeepSeek R1... with 128K-token context window" (p.6)
- Seeds: R1 has 20 seeds per task and o3 has 10 seeds per task. quote: "Methods utilizing R1 are averaged over 20 seeds per task and methods utilising o3 are averaged over 10 seeds per task" (Fig 14 caption, p.31). The Fig 13 caption agrees: "across 20 seeds withR1 and 10 seeds o3".
- The 90-hour run in App C used only 10 seeds per task ("10 independent runs per task").
- Hardware: H200, 24 CPU cores, 100 GB RAM, 1 TB scratch; 24h hard cap, 4h per execution, 5-minute grace (App E). Sampling: temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95.
- MCTS: num_children=5, uct_c=0.25. Evo: candidates_per_generation=5. Debug cycle capped at 10 nodes or 12h.
- Table 2 full 75-task set, with o3, 20 seeds: AIRA Greedy o3 31.6 ± 0.8 overall, against AIDE Greedy (o1-preview) 16.9 ± 1.1 (reproduced from prior work).
  Quote: "We achieve an overall medal rate of 31.6%". Splits: Low 55.0, Medium 22.0, High 21.7, MLE-bench-30 25.8 ± 1.3.
- Headline: 39.6% to 47.7%. The abstract's baseline 39.6 does not match Fig 3's AIDE-R1 39.77. The 39.6 appears to be the AIDE-Evo bar (39.61), which is odd. I could not reconcile this.

Other claims worth keeping from the appendices
- Operator ablations were not isolated: AIRA operators differ from AIDE in three ways (adaptive complexity, scoped memory, think tokens). Think tokens give about 2x completion tokens. Fig 10 draft tokens: AIDE 4227.7, Evo 8081.0, Greedy 8192.8, MCTS 7986.8. The extraction gives these values in that x-order, so they are my reading.
- Table 3 (full MLE-bench, AIRA-Greedy o3, 20 seeds) shows high per-task bimodality. Many tasks are 0.0 ± 0.0, for example new-york-city-taxi-fare-prediction, dog-breed-identification, and siim-isic-melanoma-classification. Others are 100: detecting-insults, predict-volcanic-eruptions, and iwildcam-2019. Examples with gold below bronze: hotel-id-2021 85/40/0 (bronze/silver/gold) and herbarium-2020 70/30/0.

LIMITS
- The authors concede the following. Operators are LLM-only; there are no agent operators and no fine-tuning. Scaling is limited to 1 GPU and 24h, and the 90h and 120h runs show overfitting. Data contamination is possible. R1 was used for the main results for rate-limit reasons, and o1-preview was only run for one agent.
- Not shown: no operator-by-operator ablation, and no experiment with a better selection method than the test oracle. Top-k assumes multiple submissions are allowed, which is not the standard benchmark rule. Fig 6 uses only the R1 agents.
- The text conflicts with itself on 15h vs 19h divergence, on 90h vs 120h in App C, and on 12.4 vs the figure arithmetic of 12.0.
- Dated: o1-preview is deprecated. R&D-Agent is concurrent work, and the authors say "Our results fall within their reported standard deviation."

BUILDS ON: AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025); MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025); MCTS (Kocsis and Szepesvári, 2006); DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025); the evolutionary-search lineage (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Hazra et al., 2025). Related: AI Scientist v2 (Yamada et al., 2025), SWE-search (Antoniades et al., 2025), Agent K (Grosnit et al., 2024). Infrastructure lessons cite Kokolis et al. (2025) for a mean time to failure of about 1000 hours per node.

CODE
- App E.1, MCTS backup (p.20): "N(u) ← N(u) + 1, Q(u) ← Q(u) + (F(vℓ) − Q(u)) / N(u)". Leaf init is N=1, Q=F; there are no roll-outs.
- Sec 4.2 selection: hUCT(v|u) = Q(v) + c·sqrt(log N(u) / (N(v)+ε)). The text extraction renders it garbled, but the form is standard.
- Evo parent selection (p.7): "πsel(v) = F(v) / Σ_u F(u)" (fitness-proportional).
- Prompt templates E.2 to E.6 (pp.20-26) are Jinja with the variables {{task_desc}}, {{memory}}, {{data_overview}}, {{prev_code}}, {{execution_output}} and {{packages}}. There are blocks like `{% if draft_complexity =='simple' %}` and `improve_complexity` with simple, normal and complex. Complexity is set by the child count n_c (<2 minimal, <4 moderate, otherwise advanced). The text writes "nc ≥ 5", which leaves n_c=4 undefined; this is a typo in the paper. The Debug prompt says "Do NOT alter the core method or underlying idea. Only correct existing bugs." Crossover parents are "sampled from the distribution of all nodes' fitness scores". All prompts require 5-fold CV score printing and a submission.csv, with no EDA.

FIGURES
- Fig 6a/b (p.10): grouped bars for Val/Val, Val/Test and Test/Test, plus medal rate against k. This is the clearest evidence for claim (a).
- Fig 3 (p.7): the AIDE-operator ablation. Flat bars show claim (b).
- Fig 4a (p.8): validation vs test curves over 24h, the widening gap.
- Fig 9 (p.17) and Fig 13 (p.30): the same gap curves for long runs and for the AIRA operators.
- Fig 11 (p.28): ranking instability by seed count.
- Fig 5 (p.9): medal rates with CIs.

PROBLEMS: None of the extraction is garbled apart from the equation and bar-label ordering in the figure text (inferred above). No embedded instructions in the PDF; the prompt templates in App E are the paper's own agent prompts, and I did not act on them. Fig 14 to 17 content is not extractable. The grep on the text file needed `-a` because of binary characters. Extracted text is at /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/aira2/full.txt.
